19.text:
MerkleForge started as fast, correct Merkle trees for blockchains. The same idea, a 32-byte root
that commits to a large dataset plus small proofs anyone can check, applies anywhere data has to be
trusted without being re-downloaded: files, logs, databases, machine-learning datasets and models,
and zero-knowledge circuits. This page is where we are taking MerkleForge across CPU, GPU,
ZK, and AI systems. Plans are grouped as Now (in review or being built), Next (designed, starting soon), and
Later (direction, open to discussion). Nothing below is a promise of a date. If something
matters to you, say so in Rust issues or
TypeScript issues, which is how items move up. Two rules hold for everything here: roots and proofs stay byte-identical across Rust, TypeScript,
and Solidity, and a faster backend never changes an output. Every new backend is tested against
the reference implementation.
19.title: Roadmap

20.text:
Three trees, one API
Binary, Sparse, and Ethereum-compatible Patricia trees in Rust (merkle-variants) and TypeScript (@merkleforge/variants), with multiproofs and byte-identical proof codecs. Ethereum and the EVM
eth_getProof verification, an OpenZeppelin drop-in, and Solidity verifiers for binary, sparse, Patricia, and Ethereum proofs. Pluggable hashes
SHA-256, Keccak-256, and BLAKE3 in both languages, plus WebAssembly Keccak-256 and SHA-256 for JavaScript. Trusted publishing
npm packages ship with provenance through npm trusted publishing; Rust vectors pin the TypeScript port in CI.
20.title: Shipped

21.text:
The fastest hash call is the one you batch. Tree builds are a sequence of independent node hashes
per layer, which is ideal for SIMD and for multiple cores. StatusItemNowBatch hashing API in TypeScript (in review): hash adapters can hash a whole tree layer in one call (hashNodePairs, hashLeaves). BinaryMerkleTree stores nodes in one flat buffer and skips hashing padding subtrees.NowNew WebAssembly backend for @merkleforge/hash-wasm: a 9 KB no_std Rust module with SIMD Keccak-256 (two permutations at once). Keccak-256 tree builds are about 5x faster than in 0.2.2 (485 ms to 98 ms at 131,072 leaves), and pure-JS tree builds about 3x faster, with byte-for-byte identical output (benchmarks and parity).NowCI on every runtime: the full test suite in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, and the built packages on Node.js, Deno, and Bun.NextOne-call proof verification in WebAssembly (fold the whole path in one call), batched multiproofs, and batch hashing for SparseMerkleTree updates.NextBLAKE3 in WebAssembly, and SHA-256 SIMD (multi-buffer).NextRust: multi-buffer SIMD hashing (AVX2, AVX-512, NEON) behind the same HashFunction trait, so a layer of nodes is hashed 4 to 8 at a time.LaterParallel tree builds: rayon in Rust and Web Workers in JavaScript for trees with millions of leaves.LaterEmbedded and no_std targets for merkle-variants (RISC-V, Cortex-M) for device attestation and firmware updates.
21.title: CPU and WebAssembly

22.text:
Large trees (10⁸ leaves and more: rollup state, data availability, dataset commitments) spend
nearly all their time hashing. The batch API above is shaped for GPUs on purpose: one layer is one
dispatch of independent pair hashes. StatusItemNextWebGPU backend for the browser and Deno: a HashFunction whose hashNodePairs runs Keccak-256, SHA-256, and Poseidon2 compute shaders. Same digests, tested against the CPU adapters.LaterNative GPU backend in Rust through wgpu (Vulkan, Metal, DirectX 12), with CUDA where it pays off, for building and updating very large trees.LaterPublished crossover measurements: at what tree size the GPU beats the CPU on common hardware, so the library can choose for you. The CPU stays the default.
22.title: GPU

23.text:
Zero-knowledge systems prove statements about Merkle trees inside a circuit, where Keccak-256 and
SHA-256 are expensive. They need SNARK-friendly hashes and proof formats that circuits can consume. StatusItemNextPoseidon2 and Poseidon adapters over BN254 (and other fields), with parameters that match circomlib, Noir, and gnark, so roots agree with existing circuits.NextIncremental (append-only) Merkle trees for commitments and nullifiers, the shape used by Semaphore-style anonymous signalling and privacy pools.LaterCircuit verifiers generated from the same proof format: Noir and Circom templates that verify binary and sparse MerkleForge proofs, alongside the existing Solidity verifiers.LaterInterop with proving systems (Halo2, Plonky3, SP1 and RISC Zero guests) so the Rust crates can run inside zkVMs and their proofs verify on-chain.
23.title: Zero-knowledge proofs

24.text:
Machine-learning pipelines move huge datasets and model files between parties that need to trust
them. A Merkle root is a compact, verifiable fingerprint of any of these, and a proof shows that
one piece belongs without sharing the rest. StatusItemNextDataset commitments: commit to a training or evaluation set (one leaf per example or shard), then prove a specific example was or was not included, for audits, licensing, and contamination checks.NextModel and checkpoint integrity: a root over fixed-size chunks of model weights, so downloads verify chunk by chunk and a corrupted or swapped shard is caught before loading. Try it with the file integrity demo.LaterVerifiable AI agent and inference logs: an append-only log of prompts, tool calls, and outputs with consistency proofs, so anyone can check the log was never rewritten.LaterRetrieval provenance (RAG): prove that a retrieved passage comes from a committed corpus version.LaterPython bindings (PyO3) so data and ML tooling can use the Rust crates directly.
24.title: AI and data systems

38.text:
MerkleForge is a framework for authenticated data structures, available as Rust crates and
TypeScript packages. You put data in, get a 32-byte root out, and hand out small proofs that
anyone holding the root can check, without downloading the rest of the data.
38.title: Why MerkleForge

39.text:
Data verification is one of the major bottlenecks in modern blockchain networks. As systems
process millions of transactions, checking the integrity of state data gets slow and
resource-intensive. Every state lookup, transaction batch, and light-client proof depends on the
speed and correctness of the underlying data structure. The Rust ecosystem has strong cryptographic building blocks, but Merkle tree support is spread
across variant-specific crates. Libraries like rs-merkle focus on binary trees, while
Ethereum-specific tries are maintained separately. Teams end up stitching together tools with
different APIs, documentation depth, test coverage, and benchmark methodology. JavaScript and TypeScript have the same gap. Libraries like merkletreejs and
@openzeppelin/merkle-tree focus on binary trees, while Ethereum-compatible tries are maintained
separately. Teams end up stitching together tools with different APIs, proof formats, and test
coverage, and proofs made in one language rarely verify in another.
39.title: The problem

40.text:
MerkleForge unifies the three Merkle tree variants used across production systems behind one
API: VariantTypical useBinaryMerkleTree<H>Transaction batching, Bitcoin-style SPV, logs, file chunksSparseMerkleTree<H>Account state, key-value maps, Layer-2 rollupsMerklePatriciaTrie<H>Ethereum state roots, receipts, storage witnesses All three are generic over a HashFunction, implement the shared
MerkleTree<H> trait, and produce proofs that verify statelessly. VariantTypical useBinaryMerkleTreeTransaction batching, airdrops and allowlists, logs, file chunksSparseMerkleTreeAccount state, key-value maps, Layer-2 rollupsMerklePatriciaTrieEthereum state roots, receipts, storage witnesses All three take a HashFunction object at construction, implement
the shared MerkleTree interface, and produce proofs that verify statelessly.
40.title: The solution

41.text:

parameter. Generics are monomorphised at compile time, so there is no runtime dispatch.Stateless verification. A light client verifies a leaf with the trusted root, the proof, and
the leaf bytes. See Proofs & stateless verification.Domain separation built in. Leaves hash as H(0x00 ‖ data) and internal nodes as
H(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right), which blocks second-preimage attacks. See the

45.text:
Every use case below has the same shape: someone commits to a lot of data with one 32-byte
root, publishes or signs that root, and later hands out small proofs that a specific piece
is (or is not) part of it. Whoever checks the proof needs only the root, the piece, and the proof,
not the rest of the data. Each section names the tree, hash, and packages to use. Items marked planned are on the
roadmap and not in the libraries yet.
45.title: Use cases

46.text:
Commit a list of (address, amount) pairs on-chain as one root, and let each user claim with a
proof. Nobody stores the full list on-chain, and gas stays constant as the list grows. Tree: StandardMerkleTree from @merkleforge/openzeppelin (same roots and proofs as
@openzeppelin/merkle-tree), or BinaryMerkleTree with Keccak256 and the MerkleForge
Solidity verifier.Verify on-chain: OpenZeppelin's MerkleProof.verify, or the MerkleForge verifiers in
contracts/.Try it: airdrop claim demo.
46.title: Airdrops, allowlists, and claims

47.title: Light clients and Ethereum state proofs

48.text:
Keep account or application state as a key-value map, prove reads, and prove a key is absent. Tree: SparseMerkleTree (membership and non-membership proofs over 32-byte keys).Hash: Sha256 or Blake3 off-chain, Keccak256 when proofs are checked by Solidity.
SNARK-friendly hashes such as Poseidon2 are planned for proofs checked inside circuits.
48.title: Rollup and app-chain state

49.text:
Commit a batch of transactions or messages, post the root, and prove inclusion of any one of them
on the other side, one at a time or with a multiproof. Tree: BinaryMerkleTree, generateMultiProof for many items at once.
49.title: Transaction batches, receipts, and bridges

50.text:
Split a file into fixed-size chunks and commit to them. A downloader that trusts only the root can
verify every chunk as it arrives, from any mirror or peer, and pinpoint a corrupted chunk instead of
re-downloading the whole file. This is how BitTorrent v2 and content-addressed storage work. Tree: BinaryMerkleTree, one leaf per chunk, Sha256 or Blake3.Try it: file integrity demo, which runs on a file you pick without uploading it.
50.title: File integrity and chunked downloads

51.text:
Publish a root over revoked certificate or credential IDs. A verifier can check a membership proof
(revoked) or a non-membership proof (still valid) without downloading the whole list. Tree: SparseMerkleTree, keyed by a hash of the ID.Try it: revocation list demo.
51.title: Revocation lists and allowlists with "not in the list" proofs

52.text:
Append events to a log and publish its root, so anyone can check an entry is in the log. Certificate
Transparency uses this to catch mis-issued TLS certificates. Today: BinaryMerkleTree gives inclusion proofs for a log you rebuild or append to.Planned: RFC 9162 append-only trees with consistency proofs (proof that a newer log extends
an older one without rewriting it).
52.title: Transparency and audit logs

53.text:
Compare two replicas of a dataset by comparing roots, then walk down only the subtrees that differ.
Serve reads with a proof so clients can check them against a root they trust. Tree: SparseMerkleTree for key-value data, BinaryMerkleTree for ordered data.Planned: replica diffing helpers and on-disk authenticated storage.
53.title: Databases and replicas

54.text:
Publish a root over a training or evaluation set, one leaf per example or shard. Later, prove a
given example was in the set (for licensing and attribution), or with a sparse tree prove it was
not (for test-set contamination checks), without releasing the dataset. Tree: BinaryMerkleTree for an ordered list of shards, SparseMerkleTree keyed by a hash of
each example when you need non-membership proofs.Planned: dataset tooling and Python bindings.
54.title: Dataset commitments

55.text:
Commit to a model file in fixed-size chunks. Mirrors and caches can serve the chunks, and a loader
verifies each one against the published root before using it, so a corrupted or swapped shard is
caught early. Tree: BinaryMerkleTree with Sha256 or Blake3, exactly as in the
file integrity demo.Planned: GPU-accelerated builds for very large checkpoints.
55.title: Model weights and checkpoints

56.text:
Record prompts, tool calls, and outputs of an AI system in an append-only log and publish its root,
so the operator cannot quietly rewrite history. Today: BinaryMerkleTree inclusion proofs over log entries.Planned: append-only trees with consistency proofs.
56.title: Agent and inference logs

57.text:
Prove "I am in this group" or "I own a note in this pool" inside a zero-knowledge proof, without
revealing which member. These systems use Merkle trees with SNARK-friendly hashes. Planned: Poseidon2 adapters, incremental append-only trees, and Noir and Circom verifiers
generated from MerkleForge proof formats. See the roadmap.
57.title: Anonymous membership and private claims

58.text:
If you are unsure which tree fits, start with Choosing a tree. In
short: an ordered list proved by position is a BinaryMerkleTree; a key-value map that needs "not
present" proofs is a SparseMerkleTree; anything that must match Ethereum roots is a
MerklePatriciaTrie with Keccak256.
58.title: Picking a tree

59.text:
Think of a Merkle root as a fingerprint for many values. Change any value and the fingerprint
changes. A proof is the short path that lets another machine check one value against that
fingerprint.
59.title: Mental model

60.title: The four pieces

61.text:
The prover (a server, indexer, or full node) holds the full tree. It publishes the root and
answers proof requests.The verifier (a light client, browser, contract, or embedded device) holds only a trusted
root, for example from a block header or a signed checkpoint. A proof is only as good as the root you check it against. Get the root from a source you trust.
61.title: Who holds what

62.text:
MerkleForge hashes leaves and internal nodes in different domains: HashPre-imageLeafH(0x00 ‖ data)Internal nodeH(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right) Without the prefixes, an internal node's pre-image (left ‖ right, 64 bytes) is also a valid leaf
value. An attacker could then present an internal node as if it were a leaf and forge a "proof"
for data that was never inserted. This is a second-preimage attack. With distinct prefixes, a
leaf hash can never equal an internal node hash for a different structure. The Sha256 and Keccak256 adapters use the byte prefixes above. Blake3 gets the same
separation from BLAKE3's derive_key mode with two context strings. See
Hash functions for the exact constructions.
62.title: Domain separation: 0x00 and 0x01

63.title: Verifying by hand

64.text:
BinaryMerkleTree pads the leaf layer to the next power of two with H::empty()hasher.empty(),
the hash of an empty leaf. Five leaves become eight slots.SparseMerkleTree has 2²⁵⁶ slots and precomputes the root of an empty subtree at every level,
so empty regions cost nothing to store.MerklePatriciaTrie follows Ethereum's node layout and has no padding. Because empty slots hash to H::empty()hasher.empty(), empty leaf data is rejected with
MerkleError::EmptyLeafDataa MerkleError with code 'EmptyLeafData'; otherwise an inserted empty value would be indistinguishable from
padding.
64.title: Padding and empty slots

65.text:
MerkleProof::leaf_countMerkleProof.leafCount tells the verifier how deep the path should be. The root does not
commit to it, so any count with the same padded size verifies. If the exact number of leaves matters
to you, get it from a trusted source and compare.

139.text:
Fallible MerkleForge operations report a MerkleError. Verification functions return a boolean
instead: a bad proof is an expected outcome, not an error. Every fallible MerkleForge API returns Result<T, MerkleError>. MerkleError lives in merkle_core::error (and the prelude). It implements Debug, Clone,
PartialEq, Eq, Display, and, with the default std feature, std::error::Error, so it works
with ?, Box<dyn Error>, anyhow, and thiserror. Every fallible MerkleForge API throws a MerkleError. It is exported from @merkleforge/core and
extends the built-in Error, so try/catch, instanceof Error, and error reporting tools work
as usual. Each error carries a detail object whose code names the case (also available as
error.code), plus that case's fields. isMerkleError(error, code?) is a type guard that narrows
detail to the given code.

proof yourself for the MerkleForgeSparse contract in
MerkleForge-ts/contracts. A Keccak-256 sparse proof carries 256 siblings, most of them empty. toSoliditySparseProof
drops the empty ones and records which levels are present in a bitmap, producing the arguments
for MerkleForgeSparse.verifyMembership / verifyNonMembership (see
contracts/). Values are
0x hex strings and a bigint, ready for viem or ethers. import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
import { SparseMerkleTree, toSoliditySparseProof } from '@merkleforge/variants'

const state = new SparseMerkleTree(Keccak256)
const alice = Keccak256.hash(utf8('alice'))
state.insert(alice, utf8('balance:100'))
state.insert(Keccak256.hash(utf8('bob')), utf8('balance:250'))

const proof = toSoliditySparseProof(state.generateMembershipProof(alice))
// Only the one non-empty sibling is kept; bit `level` of `bitmap` marks where it sits.
console.assert(proof.siblings.length === 1)
console.log(proof)

214.text:
Peer-to-peer and content-addressed systems (BitTorrent v2, IPFS, software update and backup
tools) split a file into chunks and publish the Merkle root of the chunk hashes. A downloader
that knows only the root can fetch chunks from untrusted peers in any order, check each one with
a short proof the moment it arrives, and refetch just the chunk that fails, without waiting for
the whole file. This demo splits a file into 64 KiB chunks and builds a BinaryMerkleTree with SHA-256 from

to the pure-JS adapter if WebAssembly is unavailable). Your file is read locally and never

222.text:
A server commits rows to a Merkle root and sends one row plus its proof to a client. The client
holds only the trusted root. Edit the rows, pick one to prove, then change the claimed value to

224.text:
Certificate authorities, verifiable-credential issuers, and API gateways need to answer "has this
been revoked?" for parties that should not download the whole list. A sparse Merkle tree puts
every possible ID at a fixed position (here keccak256(id)), so the issuer can publish one root
and hand out a short proof for either answer: membership: the ID is in the tree, so it is revoked;non-membership: the ID's slot is empty, so it is not revoked. The demo runs SparseMerkleTree from
@merkleforge/variants with Keccak-256.
Revoke and reinstate IDs, then check one; the proof is verified against the root alone.
224.title: Revocation list

225.text:
import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
import { keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/ethereum'
import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
import { SparseMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

const REVOKED = utf8('revoked')
const key = (id: string) => keccak256(utf8(id))

const list = new SparseMerkleTree(Keccak256)
list.insert(key('cert-2041'), REVOKED)
const root = list.root()! // publish this

const yes = list.generateMembershipProof(key('cert-2041'))
const no = list.generateMembershipProof(key('cert-1000')) // leaf: null, a non-membership proof
console.log(SparseMerkleTree.verifyMembership(Keccak256, root, key('cert-2041'), REVOKED, yes))
console.log(SparseMerkleTree.verifyNonMembership(Keccak256, root, key('cert-1000'), no)) true
true The same tree type backs account state in rollups and nullifier sets in privacy protocols. See the
sparse Merkle tree guide.
